title: The buried picnic
translation: At Ninnaji there was a very pretty boy who served at the abbot's palace, and some of the priests were plotting how to get him out for a day of fun. They brought in a few other priests who were good at livening up a party, made a fancy picnic in proper lunch boxes, and packed it all neatly into a sort of case. They buried it at a handy spot on the hill next to the temple and scattered autumn leaves over it, so nobody would ever guess. Then they went to the palace and talked the boy into coming out.

Delighted, they wandered about here and there, and then sat down in a row on the moss at the very spot. "We're exhausted," they said. "If only someone would burn some red leaves and warm us a little wine. Come on, you priests with your miraculous powers, let's see what your prayers can do." They turned to the tree where they had buried it, rubbed their prayer beads, made grand magic signs with their fingers, and really put on a show. Then they swept the leaves aside. Nothing there at all.

Maybe it was the wrong place? They dug up every inch of the hill. Nothing. Someone had watched them bury it and stolen it while they were off at the palace. The priests didn't know what to say. They had an ugly argument, got angry with each other, and went home.
If you try too hard to make something fun, it always falls flat.

literal: At Omuro there was a splendid boy, and there were priests who schemed (thinking) 'somehow let's lure him out and have fun', and they got talented entertaining priests and others to join in,

carefully prepared something like elegant partitioned lunch boxes, packed them into something box-like, buried it at a convenient place on Narabi-ga-oka, scattered autumn leaves over it and so on, so that no one would think of it, went to the palace, and coaxed the boy out.
Glad, they wandered here and there having fun, sat in a row on the moss mat they had (prepared),
and said to each other things like: 'We have become very tired. Ah, if only there were someone to burn autumn leaves. You monks who must have miraculous powers, try praying',
faced the foot of the tree where they had buried it, rubbed their rosaries, formed mudras grandly and so on, behaved pompously, and brushed away the leaves, but nothing at all could be seen.
Thinking 'is the place wrong?', they searched the hill, leaving no place undug, but it was not there.
Someone had seen them bury it and had stolen it while they had gone to the palace.
The priests had no words, quarrelled unpleasantly, got angry, and went home.
Things that try too hard to be fun are always dull.

notes.text: {御室|おむろ}: another name for Ninnaji, the temple of sections 52 and 53. Its head was usually a prince of the imperial family, and his residence was called the palace ({御所|ごしよ}).
{児|ちご}: a boy who lived and served at a temple, usually from a good family, with long hair and fine clothes. Priests admiring such boys is a common subject in the literature of the time.
Priests with a talent for entertainment: music, dancing, party tricks. The 1925 edition: priests who can add to people's fun.
{破籠|わりご}: a wooden lunch box divided into compartments. {風流|ふうりう} here means 'elaborately decorated'.
Narabi-ga-oka, a low hill right next to Ninnaji. By tradition, Kenkō lived at its foot for some time.

notes.quote: 紅葉を焼かむ人もがな
notes.text: An allusion to a line by the Chinese poet Bai Juyi, well known in Japan: 林間暖酒焼紅葉, 'in the woods we warm wine, burning red leaves'. もがな: 'if only there were'. The priests use the line as their cue for the 'miracle'.

notes.quote: 印ことごとしく結びいで
notes.text: {印|いん}: hand signs made with the fingers in esoteric Buddhism, to give a prayer power. Ninnaji is a temple of the Shingon school, where these rites are central. いらなく: 'pompously, over the top'.
つやつや … ず: 'not at all'. Not modern つやつや 'shiny'.
なりけり: 'it turned out that'. けり here marks a discovery: the explanation comes all at once.
あいなし: 'dull, no fun, pointless'. The moral is short, and the story has already made the point.
